title: Allegra Spender and Zali Steggall confirm plans to form new party
description: The teal independents have confirmed plans to form a new political party, Community Strong Australia, but are yet to convince any of their crossbench colleagues to join what they call a "responsible alternative" to the major parties.

author: Tom Crowley and Holly Tregenza
full_text: Teals Allegra Spender and Zali Steggall form new political party Community Strong Australia Thu 25 Jun 2026 at 8:45am In short: Allegra Spender and Zali Steggall are forming a new political party, Community Strong Australia. Members would retain a free vote but would "collaborate" on policy. What's next? None of the other independents in the federal parliament have said they will join the party. Independents Allegra Spender and Zali Steggall have confirmed plans to form a new political party. But they are yet to convince any of their crossbench colleagues to join what they call their "responsible alternative" to the major parties. There has long been speculation about a formal grouping of the so-called teal independents, who have won previously safe Liberal seats over the past three elections and received some funding and campaign support from the political organisation Climate 200. The pair had confirmed they were holding talks about a party in recent weeks. In a joint appearance on ABC Radio National, the pair said it would be named Community Strong Australia, but the party was yet to be formally registered and had no leaders or candidates. Party members would "collaborate" on policies, the pair said, but would retain a free vote, a model they said was "not about choosing between independents and parties but combining the strengths of both". The pair also confirmed that Climate 200 was not directly involved, with Ms Steggall saying the funding group would "remain focused on independent representation". Climate 200's ability to donate to independents across the country stands to be significantly curtailed by new electoral funding laws passed in the last parliament which Ms Steggall and Ms Spender have both suggested are biased towards political parties. A political party would have greater flexibility to prioritise resources and support multiple candidates than a collection of like-minded independents working together without a party structure. Ms Spender said wealthy donors, including Mike Cannon-Brookes and Scott Farquhar, who had given to pro-climate independents, had not been asked to be involved. Ms Steggall added it would be "for individuals who care about our politics, who will have the capacity to contribute, whether that be big or small, to enable a new choice at the table of our politics". The new electoral funding laws allow political parties to spend millions of dollars on national advertising which independents have warned will see them out-spent in their seats. Other teals yet to join Fellow teal independents Sophie Scamps and Nicolette Boele have not ruled out joining the grouping but said they would need to consult their communities. In a statement, Ms Boele congratulated the pair on their new party but confirmed she would remain an independent for now. Other independents including Monique Ryan and Kate Chaney have said they do not plan to join. ACT independent David Pocock previously ruled out joining the party and told ABC on Thursday he believed his constituents saw the "value of independence". "I'm accountable to people in the ACT," he said. "The feedback has been mixed on whether independents should actually look at forming some sort of party or alliance." Asked whether they would welcome disaffected moderate Liberals, Ms Spender said she was "open to it" but that anyone who joined would have to be "really aligned with values and … really connected to the community". Ms Steggall described the party as "centrist" but that categorising them "from a left and right perspective" was reductive, citing a focus on "sensible economic management, climate action, integrity [and] equality". Ms Spender suggested the party was for those who were pro-business but progressive on climate change. "If you're … really driving innovation, but you also support climate action, where do you go? You have no home," she said. Ms Spender has held the seat of Wentworth since 2022. It was once held by former Liberal and prime minister Malcolm Turnbull who has spoken favourably of the idea of a new centrist political party. A former economist, Ms Spender has published a "white paper" on tax which included proposals to change the tax treatment of capital gains, negative gearing and trusts. She proposed a flat capital gains tax discount of 30 per cent. Ms Steggall won her seat of Warringah in 2019 from former prime minister Tony Abbott, now the federal president of the Liberal Party. Asked why the party had no leader, Ms Steggall said that this was "a media construct of always thinking about leadership and power".
